segments.title: Why the Seven Years' War looks like a world war
segments.summary: The trailer introduces the Seven Years' War as an unusually broad case for thinking about conflict on a global scale.
segments.body: The opening asks why theorists so often begin with the Seven Years' War. It presents the conflict as a plausible first world war and as the first war to contain nearly every kind of strategic case. That combination helps explain why the conflict became a common reference point in later strategic theory. The passage states the trailer's main question before turning to land and maritime examples.

evidence.note: The introduction calls the war a possible first world war and says it contains every kind of strategic case.

segments.title: One war, contrasting land and maritime strategies
segments.summary: The Seven Years' War can support arguments about mass armies ashore as well as maritime strategy across a global theatre.
segments.body: The trailer contrasts a land-focused reading built around mass armies and huge forces fighting ashore with a maritime strategy that spans the globe. The same conflict can be used to support either case. This makes the Seven Years' War useful for comparing continental concentration with dispersed maritime reach. The comparison leads into the broader claim that a state cannot pursue either approach without accounting for demands in the other sphere.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts mass armies fighting ashore with a globe-spanning maritime strategy.

segments.title: How strategic theorists use a familiar but distant war
segments.summary: A war can become attractive to theorists when it is familiar enough to invoke but distant enough to simplify into an example.
segments.body: Many theorists approach the Seven Years' War with an argument already in mind and seek historical illustration rather than an open-ended lesson. By the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the war's name was familiar even though many of its actors and details were not. That combination made it harder for an audience to challenge a theorist with awkward context or nuance. The passage warns that a seemingly clean historical example may look persuasive because its complications are less widely known.

evidence.note: The transcript explains why theorists seek a known war whose context and nuance are less likely to be challenged.

segments.title: Why grand strategy cannot be purely maritime or continental
segments.summary: The trailer cautions that a state may lean maritime or continental, but context prevents either approach from becoming a complete answer.
segments.body: Broad strategic formulas become less convincing once the particular context of a country and war is examined. The analogy is with economic policy, where effective choices usually combine different measures. No country can afford a wholly maritime strategy, and probably no country can afford a wholly continental one. A state may make one approach its overarching priority, but it must still understand the other and remain prepared to exert some influence through it. The closing passage makes a concise case for strategic balance and the limits of broad labels.

evidence.note: The closing argument says strategic thinking runs into context and rejects wholly pure maritime or continental strategies.
